question_text: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of noble gases positive?

steps.label: The reason

steps.why: Energy is released only when the attraction of the nucleus on the added electron is greater than its repulsion by the electrons already present; in the next higher shell of a noble gas that attraction is very small, so no energy is released. Helium is the exception in form: its filled shell is 1s², with no p subshell, but the argument is the same.
common_mistakes: Saying only that noble gases are stable. The marked reason is the full ns² np⁶ shell and the next-shell entry.
Writing that noble gases cannot gain an electron at all. They can, but energy must be supplied.
steps.memory_tip: A full ns² np⁶ shell has no vacancy, so the extra electron is pushed out to the next shell.
steps.margin_note: Both parts count: the full shell, and where the added electron would have to go.

steps.label: The conclusion

lines.text: Energy must be supplied to add the electron, so the electron gain enthalpy is positive

lines: The atom does not release energy on gaining
an electron; it absorbs energy instead.
steps.why: The sign follows the direction of energy flow: released energy makes the enthalpy change negative, absorbed energy makes it positive — and for noble gases the flow is inward.
common_mistakes: Writing positive because energy is released. Released energy gives a negative enthalpy change; positive means absorbed.
steps.memory_tip: Energy in means a positive sign; energy out means a negative sign. Noble gases take energy in.
steps.margin_note: State the sign convention in one line; it is what the question is really testing.

insider_note: The sign convention is the second mark, not extra credit. A complete explanation of the filled shell that never states that energy is absorbed, and therefore the value is positive, is half an answer.
